turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through and sit yourself down. Sock and trainer off the sore foot if you can manage.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Cheers. It's the left ankle. I twisted it yesterday playing football.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Talk me through it.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, five-a-side after college, I'm on a sports course, I'm 19. Pitch was soaking, I turned, foot stuck, and there was a pop. Not a crack. Dave thought it was hilarious till I started limping, typical.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weight on it right after?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, yeah, I limped off. I can still walk on it, it just hurts, quite bad when I walk. Bus was a nightmare, two changes.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has it swollen?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Came up last night, puffy on the outside. My sister said to strap it. She takes biotin for her hair and thinks she's a pharmacist. Honestly.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave your sister's biotin. Any numbness in the toes?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bruising?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. Not a proper bruise.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fever, or feeling shivery?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. I feel fine. Had a huge pizza after, which was probably stupid.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Notes say asthma. Still a problem?

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Had it five-ish years. Blue inhaler's salbutermol, well, salbutamol, two puffs when I need it. Brown one's beclomethazone, no, beclometasone, two hundred micrograms twice a day.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does wheeze wake you at night?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes, if I've been training in the cold. Not most nights.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cough with it?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that either.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain today?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never had one.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Taken anything for the ankle?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol. Two tablets, five hundred milligrams each, this morning. My mum's on metformin for her diabetes, that's her, not me.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Smoke?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Couldn't, with the asthma, and coach would lose it. We train three times a week usually.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): On the couch, please. Tender over the outside ligament, not on the bone. Moderate swelling, and I can't see a proper bruise.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah the bone pressing is alright. Ow, front outside, that's the bit. I can feel your finger.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Foot pulses are good, toes pink, and sensation's intact where I'm touching. Pulse at the wrist is seventy-eight. Temperature's thirty-six point six degrees.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Is seventy-eight bad? I was sprinting in the warm-up, heart going mad, but that was before. And my uncle broke his ankle last year, they X-rayed him straight away.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Seventy-eight is a normal resting pulse. Your uncle's break is a different beast.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah I know, I'm not him. Go on.

[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ottawa rules, thinking aloud. You've got malleolar-area pain. I'd want an X-ray if there was bone tenderness at the back or the tip of the lateral or medial malleolus, or if you couldn't take four steps both then and now. You're tender on the ligament, not the bone, and you walked in.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Four steps is easy. It throbs after, that's all. I walked from the waiting room fine, slowly.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): So I don't think this is a fracture. Working impression is a sprain of the lateral ligament, provisional.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): So I dodge the X-ray queue?
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): No X-ray today. If it worsens, if you can't weight bear, or the pain starts climbing, then we arrange an ankle X-ray.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Fair. What do I actually do with it, then? Saturday's a cup match, I'm on the wing, Dave will be unbearable if I cry off.

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Rest, elevate it when you sit, ice in a tea towel for about ten minutes a few times a day. No football this weekend, and no training until you're walking without a limp, a week at least. Paracetamol, up to two tablets four times a day. If you need more, ibuprofen four hundred milligrams with food up to three times a day.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Ice, feet up, no wing wizardry, got it. Keep the inhalers going even if I'm not running?
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, salbutamol when you need it, beclometasone twice a day, don't stop them. If it's not clearly better in a week, book back in.

spec.situation: Young player who twisted the ankle yesterday; swelling, can bear weight with pain; doctor applies Ottawa rules aloud, no X-ray unless it worsens; rest and elevation advice.

traps.happens: The patient denies some symptoms (said as 'no', 'not really', 'never'), has a chronic condition named earlier (for example asthma or hypertension) and later the doctor asks about another symptom of it, and one answer is a double negative or a correction ('not that either', 'no... well, sometimes').
traps.label_rule: Denials go in negative_findings with the exact thing denied, never in symptoms. NEVER write a negative about a condition the patient has said they have. A corrected answer keeps only the final version. A negative is never a symptom, and 'not painful' is the finding 'pain' absent, not a symptom called 'painless'.

features: spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

bad.reason: Patient says 'not really,' not unequivocally absent bruising.
Patient says 'not really' fever, not a clear definite denial.
Patient says feels fine, but does not specifically deny shivering clearly.
Dose wording wrong: transcript says two 500 mg tablets this morning, not 500 mg total.
bad.text: paracetamol (dose=500 mg, frequency=2 tablets this morning, indication=ankle pain, status=currently_used, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: Mechanism/details of injury not recorded: foot stuck while turning on a soaking pitch during five-a-side football, with a 'pop' but not a crack.
Patient could weight bear immediately after the injury and limped off; also reported four steps was easy and walked from the waiting room slowly.
Night waking wheeze was asked and not clearly absent: patient said it happens sometimes if training in the cold, not most nights.
